title: Recent error correction lost its large gain after a valid-time check in NHC 48-hour wind forecasts in 2019-2025
abstract: We tested whether earlier signed errors can improve NHC wind forecasts when their outcomes must occur by the new issue time. Each target year used a linear fit from the previous five years. The primary common sample has 644 Atlantic cycles from 52 storms and 300 East Pacific cycles from 36 storms in 2019-2025. At a 48-hour lead, a six-hour-lag error needs an observation 42 hours in the future. This deliberately invalid control cut mean squared error by 73% and 81% against mean error correction. At lags of 48 and 72 hours, all primary whole-storm 95% limits for loss change included zero; point changes were increases of 1.79 to 4.08 kt squared. Separate available samples and earlier years support the timing contrast. A planned 72-hour-lead check showed gains in 13 East Pacific storms, so the primary null does not generalize to all leads. This is a retrospective correction benchmark, not a test of issued probabilities or an allegation of data leakage by NHC. Revised best track, long-storm selection, fixed-fit uncertainty and few test years limit use. Code, exact source hashes, aggregate evidence, a figure and an independent calculation are included.

display.caption: Paired MSE changes at 48 hours. Future-outcome correction gives a large gain; timing-valid corrections give no clear gain on identical cases. Limits resample whole storms.
